inline.s: Mr. Shen Longjiang said: ‘For a child in serving his parents, there is no greater matter than seeing them to their grave. If one cannot exhaust his heart even in this great matter of seeing his parents off, then how could he exhaust his heart in any other matter? There are those who, because the family has many brothers, shirk responsibility upon one another, and so handle the parents’ funeral in a hasty manner, leading to remorse and regret in later days. I hold that as eldest son, if one has the strength to manage it alone, one should manage it alone, and need not delegate to one’s younger brothers; and as a younger brother, if one can manage it alone, one should likewise take it as one’s own duty and not burden the elder brother too heavily; each exhausting his own heart and vying to put forth his strength — this is the way of a son! If one has in mind to rely on another even the least bit, then in his own heart there is a little place where he is not able to exhaust his heart!’

Yang Fu of Taihe took leave of his aged mother at home and went alone to Sichuan to visit Master Wuji. On the way he met an old monk, who asked Yang Fu: ‘Where are you going?’ Yang Fu replied: ‘I am going to Sichuan to visit Master Wuji.’ The old monk said: ‘Going to visit Master Wuji is not as good as going to see the Buddha!’ Yang Fu asked: ‘Then where is the Buddha?’ The old monk said: ‘If you simply go home, you will see a person with a yellow robe draped over his shoulders and wooden clogs worn backwards — that person is the Buddha!’ When Yang Fu heard this, he hurried straight back home. By the time he reached home, it was deep in the night, the stillness was profound, and the gate was already shut. Yang Fu knocked on the gate and waited outside. Then his old mother, hearing that it was her son calling from outside, was overjoyed and in her haste picked up a yellow garment and flung it over her shoulders — probably because her longing for her son had made her too excited, and when she ran out to open the gate even her wooden clogs were on backwards. As soon as Yang Fu saw his mother like this, it was exactly the appearance of the Buddha of which the old monk had spoken; and so he was suddenly awakened and enlightened. From then on he stayed at home and did his utmost in filial devotion to his mother, and he also wrote a commentary of tens of thousands of characters on the Classic of Filial Piety. While Yang Fu was commenting on the Classic of Filial Piety, the water in his inkstone was nearly dry, when suddenly the water in the inkstone brimmed full again. Everyone regarded this as a response brought about by the sincerity of Yang Fu’s filial heart, which had moved heaven and earth!

Maitreya Bodhisattva said: ‘Two honored Buddhas sit in the hall; it grieves me that the world does not know them. They are not made up with gold and color, nor carved from sandalwood; but are your parents living now, being Sakya and Maitreya. If you can serve them with sincerity and reverence, what need is there to seek merit elsewhere?’

Cui Mian was by nature extremely filial. His mother was blind in both eyes, so he sold off the family property and sought doctors everywhere to treat her eyes. He served his mother for thirty years with great respect and carefulness, not even taking off his hat and outer garment at night. Whenever a festival came, or a fine scene and beautiful day, he would certainly help his old mother to the banquet, chatting and laughing with everyone, so as to make his mother forget the pain of her blindness. Later his mother passed away, and Cui Mian was so grieved that he spat blood; he vowed to be a vegetarian for life for his mother’s sake. He loved his elder brothers and sisters as he loved his mother, and he was better to his nephews and nieces than to his own children. He divided all the salary he received among his relatives, and said: ‘Since my mother has already passed away, I have no way to express my filial heart to her. I think that while she was alive the ones she most worried about were precisely these four or five people — my elder brothers, elder sisters, nephews, and nieces. So I must treat them all well; perhaps by doing so I can comfort my mother’s spirit in heaven!’ Later Cui Mian’s official career reached the post of Vice Minister of the Secretariat, and his son Youfu became a worthy chief minister. Alas! A person like Cui Mian is truly a filial son! While his mother was alive he was able to do his utmost to make her happy, and after she passed away he was able to complete her heart’s wishes. Yet in the world there are those who, dwelling in wealth and honor, with money and power, treat their own brothers and sisters as strangers, and are unkind to their own parents and parents-in-law as though they were ordinary guests — seeing Cui Mian’s filial heart, can they not feel ashamed?

Lü Sheng lost his mother in childhood, and served his father with filial devotion. Because his father was very old and often got up at night to urinate, Lü Sheng slept with his father in order to tend him conveniently. Every night Lü Sheng rose four or five times to care for his aged father. One year when warfare and chaos came, and bandits ran rampant everywhere, Lü Sheng carried his father on his back and fled into the mountains. On the way they met robbers, but the robbers were moved by Lü Sheng’s filial heart and so did not harm the father and son. Lü Sheng’s father ordinarily loved to eat a certain sweet and fragrant kind of apricot, and for this reason Lü Sheng specially planted many apricot trees near the home. But the apricot trees he planted were forcibly seized by a neighbor. Lü Sheng, having no recourse, wrote a supplication to inform the spirits and ask for help. The spirit then punished the neighbor who had forcibly seized Lü Sheng’s apricot land, causing sores to break out on his back, and warned him, saying: ‘You must immediately return the seized apricot land to the filial son Lü Sheng!’ Only after the neighbor returned the apricot land to Lü Sheng did the spirit stop the sores on his back.

Li Jiongxiu of the Tang dynasty was by nature extremely filial. His mother had been born of humble origins, and his wife often scolded the household maidservants. When Li Jiongxiu’s mother heard this, she felt unhappy in her heart. For this reason Li Jiongxiu divorced his wife. Someone asked him: ‘For what reason did you divorce your wife?’ He said: ‘The purpose of my taking a wife was so that she would serve my mother. If my wife cannot serve my mother-in-law with gentle countenance and complete devotion, then how can I keep such a daughter-in-law at home?’ Li Jiongxiu’s filial heart moved heaven, and so in front of his hall was born a branch of the magic fungus. Emperor Zhongzong even issued a special edict commending his filial conduct.

In the Han dynasty, in Shangyu of Zhejiang, there was a girl named Cao’e. Her father, Cao Xu, was a shaman. On the day of the Dragon Boat Festival, the fifth day of the fifth month, he rode a boat on the river to welcome the spirit, and by accident fell into the river and drowned. Cao’e was only fourteen that year. She searched along the riverbank for her father’s body, but could not find it anywhere. Cao’e wept by the river for seven days and seven nights. Finally she jumped into the river, and after five days Cao’e emerged from the river carrying her father’s corpse on her back. All who saw it, near and far, were greatly shocked. The magistrate of Shangyu county, Du Shang, reported the matter to the court, and the emperor thereupon issued an edict commending Cao’e’s filial conduct, and had a shrine built for her by the riverbank. Cao’e is to this day still worshipped and honored by people.

In the Song dynasty, a filial woman of Wu lost her husband early and had no son; but she served her mother-in-law with great filial devotion. Her mother-in-law was old and had eye disease; thinking that her daughter-in-law was too lonely, she wished to adopt a son-in-law to marry her. The filial woman Wu said to her mother-in-law through tears: ‘Since ancient times, a virtuous woman does not serve two husbands; I should of course do my utmost to wait upon you, mother-in-law. Please set your mind at rest.’ Wu then did coarse manual work for the neighbors, earning some money to support her mother-in-law. If anyone gave her fine food, she would bring it home for her mother-in-law. Once, when she had not yet finished cooking the rice, a neighbor’s mother had an urgent matter and called her out to help. Her mother-in-law, worried that the rice would cook too long and scorch, put it in a box; but because her eyes were unclear, she put the rice into the trash bin. When Wu returned and saw this, she did not ask about it, but hastened to borrow some rice from a neighbor to give her mother-in-law; then she washed the soiled rice clean with water, steamed it, and ate it herself. One day she suddenly dreamed of two young boys dressed in green robes, riding clouds to come before her, holding a tally, who said: ‘We have received the jade decree of the Most High God, summoning the filial woman Wu to audience.’ When Wu saw the Most High God, he said to her: ‘You are only a village woman, yet you can be so diligent and devoted in serving your mother-in-law — truly worthy of respect! Therefore I especially bestow on you a thousand cash, to take home and support your mother-in-law; from now on you need no longer do coarse manual work to earn a living.’ Having said this, he ordered the two green-robed boys to escort Wu home. When Wu woke from the dream, she found a thousand cash indeed placed at the head of her bed; and after it was used up, a thousand cash would again appear at the head of the bed — thus round and round, endlessly continuous!

Yang Shiqi of the Ming dynasty was an elder statesman in the court, greatly favored by the emperor, holding the post of chief minister. But his son Yang Ziji, relying on his father’s influence, did all manner of evil. Yang Shiqi doted on his son and did not know he was running amok outside, until someone impeached Yang Ziji before the emperor, charging him with the great crime of killing dozens of people. The emperor then handed Yang Ziji over to judicial trial, and also specially sent a decree to console Yang Shiqi, saying: ‘My beloved minister! Your son has violated the family precepts and infringed the laws of the state. I do not dare be partial. My beloved minister, you should handle the case in accordance with justice.’ Yang Shiqi had no choice but to sentence his son to death. Yang Shiqi’s reputation was greatly damaged because his son, being unworthy, committed a capital crime and was executed. Yang Shiqi, as a scholar, rose to the lofty position of chief minister and managed the great affairs of state; yet Yang Ziji, in the status of a chief minister’s son, committed a crime and was executed, ruining the family’s name and bringing shame on his parents — one may say he had more than enough offense for death! Those arrogant, spoiled scions who run rampant relying on their fathers’ influence — seeing the fate of Yang Ziji, can they not take careful warning to themselves?

Zhang Yi every dawn very devoutly prayed to heaven, repenting the offenses he had committed in the past. One day Zhang Yi’s soul was suddenly seized by ghost-soldiers and taken to the underworld. The judge then showed him the black register recording the offenses of his whole life. In the black book were recorded all the offenses he had committed in the past; but because of his sincere repentance they had all been crossed out, with only one evil deed alone not crossed out. Zhang Yi asked the judge: ‘That one remaining offense that has not been crossed out — what kind of offense is it?’ The judge said: ‘This is because when you were small, your father scolded you, and you refused to admit your wrong, but instead glared with wide eyes and turned around to stare back at your father.’ Zhang Yi then understood that the offense of unfilial conduct does not admit of repentance!

Luo Gong, when he was a student at the Grand College, often prayed to the spirits for his future, hoping that his official career would be smooth and his prospects bright. One night he dreamed that the spirit said to him: ‘Luo Gong, you have already offended the King of the Underworld; it is best you go home quickly and ask no more about your prospects!’ Luo Gong did not understand the spirit’s meaning, so he asked the spirit again: ‘Spirit! I do not understand why you bid me go home quickly and ask no more about my prospects.’ The spirit replied: ‘Your parents passed away long ago, yet you have delayed to this day without burying them — this is an act of great unfiliality, and the King of the Underworld has already recorded your offense and is about to punish you!’ Luo Gong said: ‘I have an elder brother! He should be the one responsible for burying our parents. Why does the King of the Underworld single me out for blame?’ The spirit said: ‘Your elder brother is but an ordinary, mediocre mortal, and so is not worth blaming; whereas you are a scholar who understands the principles of the sages, and so the King of the Underworld must punish you!’ Strange to say, Luo Gong died that very year!
End of Volume One of the Vernacular Condensed Edition of the Compilation of the Tract on Response and Retribution
